analysis.one_liner: Ends tax write-offs for cutting old-growth redwood and taxes the cutting itself.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the tax code so that logging companies could no longer deduct the costs of cutting old-growth redwood — trees at least 150 years old — or redwood that had been used as collateral for corporate debt. It would also charge a 75% tax, based on the timber's market value, on cutting any such tree, making old-growth redwood logging economically impossible. The bill was sent to the tax-writing committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people and future generations who would keep the remaining old-growth redwood forests standing. Redwoods can live for over a thousand years and are found almost nowhere else on Earth; the bill's deduction denial and 75% cutting tax were designed to make harvesting ancient trees uneconomical on private land, which was where the bulk of remaining old-growth stood.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone with a stake in old-growth redwood forests

how_it_helps.text: The bill denies income tax deductions for any expense connected with cutting redwood timber on tracts where at least 10% of the redwood trees are 150 years old or older, including depreciation and depletion allowances.

It also denies deductions for cutting 'disqualified securitized redwood timber' — redwood pledged as collateral for, or generating payments on, publicly offered debt issued on or after March 12, 1993 — targeting logging financed by borrowed money rather than long-term stewardship.

It imposes an excise tax equal to 75% of the fair market value of the timber, paid by whoever holds the economic interest, on cutting old-growth or securitized redwood, which would make such cutting a losing proposition financially.
Both provisions take effect immediately upon enactment — the deduction denial applies to expenses after enactment and the excise tax to timber cut after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and investors holding economic interests in old-growth or securitized redwood. They would lose existing tax write-offs and face a 75% tax on the market value of any old-growth redwood they cut. Logging jobs in the redwood region and lumber supply could be affected at the margin, though the bill leaves all non-old-growth, non-securitized redwood cutting untouched.
analysis.who_pays_short: Redwood timber companies and timber-debt investors

drawbacks.text: The 75%-of-market-value excise tax is so high it effectively bans cutting old-growth redwood on private land, which owners and timber interests would object to as confiscatory treatment of private property.

The bill is aimed at one species in one region, so it would concentrate economic pain on redwood-country loggers, mills, and timberland owners while leaving similar old-growth cutting in other forest types untouched.
Restricting old-growth redwood harvest would reduce timber supply from those tracts, with some effect on regional logging employment and lumber prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill asked a small, identifiable group — redwood timber operators and the investors behind securitized redwood deals — to give up tax subsidies and absorb a prohibitive cutting tax, in exchange for protecting trees that take centuries to replace and that provide benefits everyone shares. The property-rights and regional-jobs objections are real, but the tax code currently treats ancient forest the same as any timber, effectively subsidizing its conversion to lumber. The design is narrow but the trade is defensible; the main honest criticism is that a 75% tax is a prohibition, not a policy calibrated to balance harvest and preservation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill in the House on March 18, 1993 and gave introductory remarks the same day.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law, on the day of introduction.
No further action was taken — the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Redwood timber operators and holders of securitized redwood debt were better off: they kept their tax deductions for cutting old-growth trees and faced no 75% cutting tax. The remaining old-growth redwood on private land stayed available for harvest.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Redwood timber operators and timber-backed debt investors

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on March 18, 1993.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never took it up — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history before the Congress ended.

against.name: The timber and timber-finance interests the bill targeted
against.role: Redwood timber companies and investors in securitized redwood timber
against.what_they_did: No cosponsor stepped forward, and no other member of the House picked the bill up; the industry-facing provisions drew no champion in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of any party, and never came to a vote, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: They would lose deductions for cutting old-growth trees and pay a 75% market-value tax on any such cut, which would end old-growth redwood logging as a business. Their gain from the bill's death was keeping the status quo, in which the tax code treats 150-year-old trees like any other asset.

industries.industry: Investors in securitized redwood timber debt
industries.note: The bill targets redwood pledged against publicly offered debt issued after March 12, 1993, denying deductions where logging proceeds pay off bondholders. These investors' returns depended on cutting the collateral trees.

industries.industry: Northern California logging and milling communities
industries.note: Restricting old-growth harvest would cost some regional logging and mill jobs, though the bill leaves all other redwood and timber operations untouched.
